This includes conducting a data protection impact assessment where necessary and ensuring that the default settings of systems and services provide adequate protection for personal data. This is mandated by Article 25 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

Pseudonymisation under the GDPR refers to the processing of personal data in such a way that the data subject can no longer be identified without additional information, which must be kept separately and subject to strict conditions. This is defined in Article 28 of the GDPR.

Consent to processing can be withdrawn at any time, and this must be done in a manner that is easily accessible and understandable. The withdrawal of consent must be facilitated without undue difficulty, and the controller must provide clear information on how to withdraw consent. This is in line with Article 17 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

A contract between a controller and a processor must contain the essential elements as set out in Article 28 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). These include the purpose and scope of the processing, the nature, scope, timing, and purpose of the processing activities, the types of personal data and categories of data subjects, the obligations and rights of the controller and the processor, the security measures, and the terms for the processor's termination and the transfer of personal data. The contract must also be in writing and must be concluded in accordance with the GDPR.

Both regulations aim to protect individuals and ensure the ethical use of technology.

qwen2.5-coder_7b__rag.answer: An AI system is a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment. It infers from input to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. The objectives can be explicit or implicit, and the system operates in various environments.

A deployer is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity.

A 'provider' is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge (Article 3(3)).
No, social scoring of people by AI systems is not allowed under the AI Act.
No, an employer cannot use AI to infer the emotions of its employees at work unless the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons.
No, it is not allowed to build a facial recognition database by scraping facial images from the internet.

Police may use real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement for any of the objectives referred to in paragraph 1, first subparagraph, point (h), and it shall take into account the following elements: the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm that would be caused if the system were not used; the consequences of the use of the system for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of those consequences.

An AI system that is a safety component of a product is considered high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or if the AI system itself is a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and if the product undergoes a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I.

An AI system listed in Annex III is nevertheless not considered high-risk if it meets the conditions set out in Article 6(3) of the AI Act. These conditions include performing narrow procedural tasks, improving the result of a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing human assessment, or being a preparatory task for certain assessments. Additionally, an AI system is not considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons.

Yes, an AI tool that screens and filters job applications is a high-risk AI system as it falls under the category of AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, which is explicitly listed in Article 6(2)(a) of the AI Act.

A risk management system for a high-risk AI system must include the identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, the estimation and evaluation of risks under intended and foreseeable misuse, the evaluation of other risks from post-market monitoring, and the adoption of appropriate risk management measures. It must also ensure that residual risks are acceptable, considering elimination or reduction of risks through design and development, and providing necessary information and training. The system must be documented and regularly reviewed and updated.

Training, validation and testing data sets for high-risk AI systems must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They should have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. Data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system should include relevant design choices, data collection processes, data-preparation processing operations, an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets, examination of possible biases, appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate biases, and the identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings. These requirements are necessary to effectively mitigate the risks for health, safety and fundamental rights.
Yes, high-risk AI systems must automatically log events over their lifetime.

Human oversight for high-risk AI systems aims to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights when the system is used in accordance with its intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse. It ensures that natural persons can oversee the system's functioning, understand its capacities and limitations, monitor its operation, and intervene if necessary. This includes addressing anomalies, dysfunctions, and unexpected performance, as well as preventing automation bias and ensuring the correct interpretation of the system's output. Human oversight measures should be designed to be appropriate and proportionate, and they may include in-built operational constraints and mechanisms to guide and inform the operator on when and how to intervene. For certain biometric identification systems, an enhanced human oversight requirement may be necessary, requiring separate verification by at least two natural persons. This requirement should not pose unnecessary burdens or delays.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, and deployers of certain high-risk AI systems listed in an annex to this Regulation, such as banking or insurance entities, should carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment prior to putting it into use.

Yes, providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must ensure that the natural persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. This obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties.

Deployers must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. For artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works, disclosure must be limited to an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 10^25.

Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation. This documentation must contain, at a minimum, the information set out in Annex XI for the purpose of providing it, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities. They must also draw up, keep up-to-date and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the general-purpose AI model into their AI systems, containing elements set out in Annex XII. Additionally, providers must ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk and the physical infrastructure of the model. Compliance should be proportionate to the type of model provider, with simplified ways of compliance allowed for SMEs. In the case of modifications or fine-tuning, the obligations should be limited to that modification or fine-tuning.
The maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice is EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the offending entity, whichever is higher.

The supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.
The maximum fine for providers of general-purpose AI models is 3% of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher.

A provider must report a serious incident caused by a high-risk AI system immediately after establishing a causal link or reasonable likelihood of such a link, and not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the incident. The period may be shortened in certain cases, such as for widespread infringements or deaths, where the report must be provided immediately and within two days, respectively.
No, the AI Act does not apply to AI systems used exclusively for military purposes.
No, an AI model developed only for scientific research is not covered by the AI Act.

Yes, a person affected by a decision based on a high-risk AI system has the right to an explanation. This right is provided under Article 86(1) of the AI Act, which states that affected persons have the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system must contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV, including the identity and contact details of the provider, the characteristics, capabilities, and limitations of performance of the AI system, changes to the system and its performance, human oversight measures, computational and hardware resources needed, and the expected lifetime of the AI system. It should also include information on the intended purpose, level of accuracy, known and foreseeable circumstances, technical capabilities, performance regarding specific persons or groups, input data specifications, and information to enable deployers to interpret the output. For products covered by Union harmonisation legislation, a single set of technical documentation containing all these elements must be drawn up.

For a high-risk biometric AI system when the provider has applied harmonised standards, the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control as referred to in Annex VI applies. This is because biometric systems are excluded from the scope of third-party conformity assessment under the AI Act.
A provider of a high-risk AI system has to register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71.

The post-market monitoring system of a high-risk AI system must actively and systematically collect, document, and analyze relevant data which may be provided by deployers or collected through other sources on the performance of the AI system throughout its lifetime, and which allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of the AI system with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. It should also include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law-enforcement authorities.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure their systems comply with the requirements set out in Section 2, indicate their name and contact details, have a quality management system, keep necessary documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking, comply with registration obligations, take corrective actions, and demonstrate conformity upon request. They must also ensure accessibility requirements are met. These obligations are detailed in Articles 16, 17, 20, and 21 of the AI Act.

A controller must notify a personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it. However, this can be delayed if the controller can demonstrate that the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. If the notification cannot be made within 72 hours, the reasons for the delay should accompany the notification.

Data subjects must be told about a personal data breach when it is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. This must be done without undue delay. The controller should communicate the breach to the data subject, and this communication should describe the nature of the breach and provide recommendations to mitigate potential adverse effects. The controller should cooperate with the supervisory authority and respect guidance provided by it. If the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures to render the personal data unintelligible or has taken subsequent measures to mitigate the risk, communication to the data subject may not be required. If communication is not required, a public communication or similar measure should be used instead.
The maximum GDPR fine for violating the basic principles of processing is 20 000 000 EUR, or 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

Controllers who breach their obligations on data protection by design or on records of processing may be subject to an administrative fine up to 10 000 000 EUR or 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, as per Article 83(4) of the GDPR.

A data subject can ask for their personal data to be erased based on the following grounds: the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed; the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based; the data subject objects to the processing; the personal data have been unlawfully processed; the personal data have to be erased for compliance with a legal obligation; or the personal data have been collected in relation to the offer of information society services. These grounds are set out in Article 17(1) of the GDPR.

A data protection officer must be designated in any case where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity; or where the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or where the core activities of the controller or the processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10. In the AI Act, a 'provider' refers to the natural or legal person, public authority, body, or other body which offers AI systems to the public or to third parties for use. This includes both providers of AI systems and providers of AI tools.

Such processing could be considered sensitive personal data under the GDPR, requiring a higher standard of justification, including a legitimate interest assessment and a balancing test against the rights and freedoms of the employees.

No, building a facial recognition database by scraping facial images from the internet would likely violate the GDPR, as it involves processing personal data without consent and could infringe on individuals' privacy rights. Article 5(1)(a) of the GDPR requires that personal data are processed lawfully, fairly, and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject. Article 6(1)(a) requires that processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is a party or to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract.

The GDPR also applies, particularly Articles 6 and 9, which require a legal basis and proportionality for such processing activities.

An AI system that is a safety component of a product is considered high-risk under the AI Act if it is related to essential infrastructure, transport, health, energy, or public safety, and if it poses a risk to the safety or the rights and freedoms of natural persons. These conditions are specified in Article 4(1)(a) and (b) of the AI Act.

An AI system listed in Annex III of the EU AI Act is generally considered high-risk. However, it may not be considered high-risk if it does not pose a risk to the safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, as determined by the Commission through a delegated act. Job application screening falls under the category of AI systems for employment, workers, or education, which are subject to high-risk classification.

A risk management system for a high-risk AI system must include the identification, analysis, and mitigation of risks, as well as the monitoring of the AI system's performance and the updating of the risk management system as necessary. This is in accordance with Article 62(1) of the EU AI Act.

For high-risk AI systems, the AI Act requires that the training, validation, and testing datasets must be representative, of sufficient quality, and of sufficient quantity to ensure the accuracy, robustness, and fairness of the AI system. This is outlined in Article 11 of the AI Act.
Yes, high-risk AI systems must log events automatically according to Article 31 of the EU AI Act.

The purpose of human oversight for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act is to ensure that these systems are used in a manner that respects the rights and safety of individuals. This oversight is intended to mitigate risks and ensure compliance with legal and ethical standards. Article 6(3) of the EU AI Act outlines the requirements for human oversight.

Under the EU AI Act, deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs generated by such systems for a period of at least 10 years after the end of the provision of the AI system. This requirement is specified in Article 65(1) of the EU AI Act.
Deployers of AI systems that are categorized as high risk under the AI Act are required to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment. This obligation is specified in Article 34 of the AI Act.

Yes, according to the EU AI Act, transparent communication with users is required. The maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice under the EU AI Act is up to 30 million euros or 6% of the annual global turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is in accordance with Article 64 of the EU AI Act.

The AI Act does not specify fines for giving misleading information to a notified body. Such provisions are typically found in other EU regulations, such as the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) or the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (IVDR).

The fines for providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act can be up to 30 million euros or 6% of the annual global turnover of the provider, whichever is higher. This is in line with Article 61 of the EU AI Act.
A provider must report a serious incident caused by a high-risk AI system without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, according to Article 45(2) of the EU AI Act.

The AI Act primarily focuses on the use of AI systems in civil applications and does not cover AI systems used exclusively for military purposes. Therefore, such systems are not directly regulated by the AI Act.

Yes, a person affected by a decision based on a high-risk AI system has a right to an explanation under Article 13(1) of the EU AI Act.

The post-market monitoring system of a high-risk AI system must be designed to continuously collect and analyze data to ensure the AI system continues to operate as intended and to detect any safety, security, or ethical issues. This system must be capable of triggering corrective measures if necessary. Article 57 of the AI Act outlines these requirements.

Providers of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act are primarily obligated to ensure that their systems comply with the technical requirements and obligations set out in the regulation, including the provision of documentation, risk management, and the establishment of a human-in-the-loop system where appropriate. Under the GDPR, a data controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach. However, this does not apply if the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. See Article 33(2) of the GDPR.

Data subjects must be informed without undue delay after a personal data breach has been determined, and without undue delay after the controller has become aware of it, according to Article 34 of the GDPR.

The maximum GDPR fine for violating the basic principles of processing, such as legality, fairness, and transparency, is 20 million euros or 4% of the annual global turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is specified in Article 83(4) of the GDPR.

The GDPR does not specify a specific fine for controllers who breach their obligations on data protection by design or on records of processing. The fines are determined based on the severity of the breach and the nature of the violation, as outlined in Articles 83 and 84 of the GDPR.

A data subject can request the erasure of their personal data under Article 17 of the GDPR, also known as the 'right to be forgotten,' if the data is no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which it was collected or processed, if the data subject withdraws consent, if the data is processed for direct marketing purposes, if the data subject objects to the processing and there are no legitimate grounds for the processor to continue processing, or if the personal data has been unlawfully processed.

A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is required under the GDPR when a data processing operation is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, particularly where the processing is likely to result in a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects on an individual, and when the processing is likely to result in a decision that produces legal or similarly significant effects for the individual. Article 35 of the GDPR provides the detailed requirements and criteria for conducting a DPIA.

Under the GDPR, individuals must be at least 16 years old to consent to their own data processing. If they are younger, consent must be given by a parent or guardian. The exact age can be lowered to 13 years old by the member state, but not below this age.

The lawful bases for processing personal data under the GDPR are specified in Article 6 of the regulation. These include consent, contract fulfillment, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, and legitimate interests.

Special categories of personal data, also known as sensitive personal data, include information concerning race or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data where processed for the unique identification of a natural person, health data, and data concerning a natural person’s sex life or sexual orientation. These categories are protected under Article 9 of the GDPR.

Under the GDPR, individuals have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or significantly affects them. This right is outlined in Article 22 of the GDPR.

The right to data portability gives a data subject the right to receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format and to have it transferred directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible. This right is outlined in Article 20 of the GDPR.

Under the GDPR, a controller must respond to a data subject's access request without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receiving it. This period can be extended by two months for complex requests or those involving multiple data subjects. See Article 12(3) and Article 15(3) of the GDPR.

Small companies are required to keep records of processing activities under the GDPR, but the level of documentation can be proportionate to the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing. Article 30 of the GDPR mandates that controllers and processors keep records of processing activities, but the specific details can vary based on the company's size and the nature of the processing activities.

Data protection by design and by default requires that privacy and data protection are integrated into the processing of personal data from the onset of the project and throughout the entire lifecycle of the data. This means that appropriate technical and organizational measures are implemented to ensure a level of protection that is appropriate to the risk. The GDPR, Article 25, mandates that controllers and processors take measures to ensure that privacy is embedded in the design and offered as a default option.

Pseudonymisation under the GDPR refers to the processing of personal data in such a manner that the data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information. Article 4(5) of the GDPR defines pseudonymisation.
