This includes training and education. Article 22 of the EU AI Act outlines these requirements.
Each Member State is required to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox by the entry into force of the AI Act, which is expected to be several years after the regulation is adopted.

Yes, the AI Act could potentially cover such apps under Article 5(3), which prohibits AI systems whose primary purpose is to generate or manipulate images, videos, or audio to create false information in a way that could harm individuals or societies.

The AI Act does not specify which companies can comply with the quality management system requirements in a simplified way. The regulation focuses on the obligations of providers of AI systems, but it does not provide details on the simplification of quality management systems.
Providers of generative AI systems that are already on the market before August 2026 must comply with the machine-readable marking obligation by August 2026, as per Article 23(2) of the EU AI Act.

The AI Act does not specify different fine caps for small mid-cap enterprises (SMCs) compared to other entities. Fines are generally based on the severity of the violation and the potential harm caused, as outlined in Article 64 of the AI Act.

Yes, a fundamental rights impact assessment can reuse parts of a GDPR data protection impact assessment, as both processes aim to identify and mitigate risks to fundamental rights. However, the assessment should be tailored to the specific AI system and its context.

The prohibitions on AI-generated intimate images and child sexual abuse material are applicable as of the entry into force of the EU AI Act, which is scheduled for May 2024, subject to the completion of the legislative process and publication in the Official Journal of the European Union.
En personuppgiftsincident måste anmälas till tillsynsmyndigheten inom 72 timmar efter att den har upptäckts, enligt artikel 33 av GDPR. ​

Den högsta sanktionsavgiften för förbjudna AI-metoder enligt AI-förordningen kan upp till 6% av företagets globala bruttolönsincome från det föregående året eller 30 miljoner euro, vad det är störst. Detta gäller enligt artikel 65 i AI-förordningen.

En arbetsgivare får inte använda AI för att avläsa anställdas känslor på arbetsplatsen, eftersom detta skulle kunna rikta sig mot principen om integritet och integritet i GDPR. Detta berör också AI Act, där AI-system som kan påverka personers rättigheter och intressen måste uppfylla vissa krav, inklusive att inte skapa obehag eller skada personers hälsa.
Kraven för AI-system med hög risk enligt bilaga III tillämpas från den 16:e december 2024, vilket är datumet för inkomst i kraft för EU AI-aktorn.

Enligt GDPR kan enligt artikeln 13 krävas ett särskilt samtycke för behandling av personuppgifter för barn under åldern för självständigt samtycke, vilket ofta är 16 år eller mer, men kan variera beroende på länderna i EU. För barn under denna ålder krävs vanligtvis samtycke från en vuxen ansvarig.

En leverantör enligt AI-förordningen (EU) 2024/1689 är en organisation eller en person som kontrollerar eller bestämmer ändamålsenligen syftet och de tekniska detaljerna för AI-systemet. Artiklar 3 och 24 av AI-förordningen definierar rollerna och ansvarsområdena för leverantörer och användare.

En chattbot bör informera användaren om att den är en AI, särskilt om det påverkar användarriktigheten eller säkerheten. Denna förpliktelse finns i artikel 15 av EU AI-aktorns ramar och i GDPR, artikel 13 och 14 om transparens och information till individerna.

En AI-modell för allmänna ändamål med hög påverkansgrad antas ha minst 1 miljoner persondata eller 10 000 persondata och en minst 100 000-taliga uppsättning av data. Detta gäller enligt AI-Act artikel 12.

En registrerad rätt att få sina personuppgifter raderade upphör att gälla om personuppgifterna raderas i enlighet med lagstiftningen. Detta gäller enligt artikel 17 i GDPR, vilket kallas för rätten till radering eller 'forgetting right'.

En konsekvensbedömning avseende dataskydd måste göras när det förutsätts att en verksamhet eller en annan aktivitet kan ha en negativ effekt på de mänskliga rättigheterna och de mänskliga värdena som utgör grund för EU:s funktion som fastställd i artikel 52 GDPR. Artiklar 35-36 i GDPR beskriver kraven och processen för konsekvensbedömning.

En myndighet måste inte utse ett dataskyddsombud enligt GDPR. Artiklarna 37-39 definierar vilka organisationer som har skyldigheten att ernämna och utse ett dataskyddsombud, vilket inte inkluderar alla myndigheter.

En AI-system som sorterar jobbansökningar kan identifieras som ett AI-system med hög risk enligt AI-Actens artikel 38, om det inkluderar beslut som har eller kan ha stora effekter på personers rättigheter och friheter. Men riskkategorin avgörs av flera faktorer, inte bara typen av AI-system.

En tillhandahållare av ett AI-system med hög risk ska spara loggar i enlighet med artikel 71(2) av EU AI-aktorn, vilket anger att loggar ska sparas i en tillräckligt lång tid för att kunna underlätta efterforskning i fallet av misstänkt eller bevisat skada.

Leverantörer och tillhandahållare av AI-system har en skyldighet att ha tillräcklig kunskap om AI-systemets egenskaper och funktionalitet för att kunna identifiera potentiella risker och tillämpa nödvändiga kontroller. Denna skyldighet finns i artikel 14 av EU AI-aktorn.
The Swedish Market Surveillance Authority (Marknadsväsendets förvaltningsmyndighet, MFA) acts as the market surveillance authority for the AI Act in Sweden.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) requires online platforms to establish and implement measures to identify, remove, or disable access to illegal content promptly. This obligation is detailed in Article 17 of the DSA.

The cost of a conformity assessment by a notified body can vary significantly depending on the type of AI product, the complexity of the assessment, and the specific requirements. There is no fixed amount specified in the AI Act.

The Court of Justice of the EU in the Schrems II judgment decided that the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework was invalid for transferring personal data from the EU to the U.S. The judgment also confirmed that standard contractual clauses can be used as an adequate safeguard for data transfers, provided they are supplemented by appropriate additional measures. This decision was made under Article 46 and 47 of the GDPR.

The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) is not covered by the EU AI Act or GDPR. Therefore, the question assumes something false, as the CCPA is a U.S. law and not relevant to EU regulations. The GDPR does provide similar rights, such as the right to object to the processing of personal data for direct marketing purposes, but it does not specifically mention a 'sale' of data. For the CCPA, consumers have the right to opt out of the sale of their personal information, but this is outside the scope of the EU regulations.

The UK GDPR does not specify a maximum fine; instead, fines are determined by the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) based on the nature and severity of the breach. The UK GDPR aligns with the GDPR in terms of principles but has its own enforcement mechanisms.
Insufficient. The AI Act has not yet been enforced, as it is still in the process of being transposed into national laws. Therefore, no fines have been issued under this regulation so far.

Harmonised standards for the AI Act have not yet been published by CEN-CENELEC, as the regulation is still in the process of being adopted and implemented. Once adopted, the AI Act will reference relevant harmonised standards developed by CEN-CENELEC or other organizations, but as of now, none have been published for this specific regulation.
The EU AI Act and GDPR do not specify corporate income tax rates for AI start-ups. These matters are typically regulated by national tax laws.

I Sverige ansvarar Myndigheten för teknik- och miljövård (TMS) för tillsynen av AI-förordningen. Artiklar 71-73 av AI-förordningen bestämmer om ansvarsområden för olika myndigheter, där TMS har ansvar för tillsynen av AI-system.

Insufficient information to answer the question. The EU AI Act and GDPR do not provide details on specific fines issued by the Swedish Data Protection Authority (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten) to Spotify or any other company.

The AI Act does not specify a training-compute threshold for categorizing AI systems as high-risk. The classification is based on the intended use and the risk associated with the application, as detailed in Article 4(1) of the AI Act.

The GDPR does not specifically require a fundamental rights impact assessment for AI systems. However, Article 35 requires an impact assessment for processing operations that are likely to result in a high risk, which could include AI systems.

No, the AI Act does not ban all biometric identification; it imposes strict conditions on the use of high-risk AI systems, including biometric identification systems, which must be subject to a safety assessment and comply with certain requirements. Shops using facial recognition for security would need to ensure their systems meet these conditions.

qwen2.5_7b__rag.answer: An AI system is defined as a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment. It infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. This definition is based on key characteristics of AI systems, such as their capability to infer, and distinguishes them from simpler traditional software systems or programming approaches.

A 'deployer' under the AI Act is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity.

A 'provider' in the AI Act means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge.

Social scoring of people by AI systems is not allowed under the AI Act. According to Article 5(1)(c) and Recital 31, the AI Act prohibits the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, with the social score leading to either or both of the following: (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons in social contexts that are unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected; (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons that is unjustified or disproportionate to their social behaviour or its gravity.
No, an employer cannot use AI to infer the emotions of its employees at work, except where the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons.

No, it is not allowed to build a facial recognition database by scraping facial images from the internet. According to Recital 43 and Article 5(1)(e) of the AI Act, the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage is prohibited.

Police may use real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement, specifically to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual, as outlined in Article 5(2) of the AI Act. This use must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions, and be authorized by a fundamental rights impact assessment and registration in the EU database, unless there is a duly justified case of urgency.

An AI system that is a safety component of a product is considered high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and the product whose safety component is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I.

An AI system listed in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making. This can occur if the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, improve the result of a previously completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing human assessment, or perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the use cases listed in Annex III. However, the AI system shall always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons.

An AI tool that screens and filters job applications is considered a high-risk AI system under the AI Act, as it falls under the category of AI systems intended to be used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, as stated in AI Act Annex III, point 4(a).

A risk management system for a high-risk AI system must include the identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, the estimation and evaluation of risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, the evaluation of other risks based on data from post-market monitoring, and the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures. These measures should aim to eliminate or reduce risks as far as technically feasible, and provide information and, where appropriate, training to deployers.

Training, validation, and testing data sets for high-risk AI systems must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They should have appropriate statistical properties, including as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. These characteristics can be met at the level of individual data sets or a combination thereof (Article 10(3) AI Act). Additionally, data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system should be implemented, covering design choices, data collection processes, data preparation operations, assumptions, data availability, bias assessment, and measures to mitigate biases (Article 10(2) AI Act).
Yes, high-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.

The purpose of human oversight for high-risk AI systems is to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may emerge when such systems are used, particularly when risks persist despite the application of other requirements. This includes enabling the deployer to properly understand the system's capacities and limitations, monitor its operation, detect and address anomalies, and intervene as necessary.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data. For financial institutions subject to Union financial services law, the logs must be maintained as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant financial service law.

Deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III are required to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment.

Yes, a chatbot must inform users that they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious from the context. This obligation is subject to specific exceptions for AI systems used in law enforcement.

Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. However, this obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Additionally, where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, the transparency obligations are limited to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 10^25.

Providers of general-purpose AI models are required to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation. This documentation must contain, at a minimum, the information set out in Annex XI and should be made available, upon request, to the AI Office and the national competent authorities. Additionally, providers must draw up, keep up-to-date, and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the general-purpose AI model into their AI systems. This information should enable providers of AI systems to have a good understanding of the capabilities and limitations of the general-purpose AI model and to comply with their obligations pursuant to this Regulation. The information and documentation must contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex XII.

The maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice is up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

A fine of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, applies for giving misleading information to a notified body under the AI Act.

The Commission may impose on providers of general-purpose AI models fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher.

The provider must report a serious incident caused by a high-risk AI system immediately after establishing a causal relationship, but not later than 10 days after becoming aware of the incident. However, in the event of a widespread infringement or a serious incident, the report must be provided immediately, and not later than two days after becoming aware of it.

Yes, the AI Act applies to AI systems used exclusively for military purposes if they are placed on the market, put into service, or used for other purposes, including civilian or law enforcement purposes. If an AI system developed for military purposes is also used for civilian purposes, it falls within the scope of this Regulation.
An AI model developed only for scientific research and development is not covered by the AI Act, as it is specifically excluded from its scope.

Yes, a person affected by a decision based on a high-risk AI system has the right to an explanation. This right is provided under Article 86(1) of the AI Act, which states that any affected person subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of systems listed under point 2 thereof, and which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights, shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system must contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV, which include general characteristics, capabilities and limitations of the system, algorithms, data, training, testing and validation processes used, and documentation on the relevant risk-management system. Additionally, it must contain the elements specified in Article 11(1) and Article 13(3) of the AI Act, such as the identity and contact details of the provider, the characteristics, capabilities, and limitations of performance of the AI system, including its intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and any known or foreseeable circumstances that may impact these aspects. The documentation should also include information on human oversight measures and computational and hardware resources needed.

For a high-risk biometric AI system, where the provider has applied harmonised standards, the provider shall opt for the assessment of the quality management system and the assessment of the technical documentation, with the involvement of a notified body, referred to in Annex VII. This is because high-risk AI systems intended to be used for biometrics are an exception to the general rule and should be carried out as a general rule by the provider under its own responsibility, with the only exception of AI systems intended to be used for biometrics, which require the involvement of a notified body.

A provider of a high-risk AI system must register themselves and information about their AI system in the EU database. This includes details about the system that are relevant for high-risk AI systems as set out in an annex to the Regulation. Any substantial modification of the high-risk AI system should also be registered.

The post-market monitoring system of a high-risk AI system must actively and systematically collect, document, and analyze relevant data throughout the lifetime of the system, which may be provided by deployers or collected through other sources. This data should allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of the AI system with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. Additionally, where relevant, the system should include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. The system should not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law-enforcement authorities.

Providers of high-risk AI systems are required to ensure compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2, indicate their contact information, have a quality management system in place, keep relevant documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment, affix the CE marking, comply with registration obligations, take corrective actions, demonstrate conformity upon request, and ensure accessibility. These obligations are detailed in Articles 16, 17, 20, and 21 of the AI Act.
The controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority.

Data subjects must be informed without undue delay when the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms (Article 34(1)). However, communication is not required if appropriate technical and organisational measures render the personal data unintelligible to any person who is not authorised to access it, if subsequent measures ensure the high risk is no longer likely to materialise, or if it would involve a disproportionate effort (Article 34(3)).

The maximum GDPR fine for violating the basic principles of processing, as per Article 83(5) of the GDPR, is up to 20,000,000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

Administrative fines for controllers who breach their obligations on data protection by design or on records of processing, as outlined in Articles 25 and 30 of the GDPR, can be up to 10,000,000 EUR or 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, as per Article 83(4) of the GDPR.

A data subject can ask for their personal data to be erased based on the following grounds: the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed; the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based; the data subject objects to the processing; the personal data have been unlawfully processed; the personal data have to be erased for compliance with a legal obligation; or the personal data have been collected in relation to the offer of information society services. These grounds are outlined in Article 17(1) of the GDPR.

It is mandatory to designate a data protection officer in cases where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity; the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10.

A data protection impact assessment is required when there is systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons based on automated processing, including profiling, and on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect the natural person (Article 35(3)(a)), processing on a large scale of special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences (Article 35(3)(b)), or systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale (Article 35(3)(c)). Additionally, it should be carried out by the controller prior to processing in order to assess the particular likelihood and severity of the high risk (Recital 90).

From the age of 16, a child can consent on their own to the processing of their data by an online service. For children below 16, such processing can be lawful only if and to the extent that consent is given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child. Member States may provide for a lower age, but it must not be below 13 years.

The lawful bases for processing personal data include: (1) the consent of the data subject (Article 6(1)(a) of the GDPR); (2) the necessity for compliance with a legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c)); (3) the performance of a contract with the data subject (Article 6(1)(e)); (4) the necessity for taking steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract (Article 6(1)(f)); (5) the protection of the vital interests of the data subject or another natural person (Recital 46); (6) the legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, except where the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject override them (Recital 47); and (7) the processing necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or the exercise of official authority vested in the controller (Article 6(3)).

Special categories of personal data include racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health, and data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation. These categories are particularly sensitive and require specific protection.

Yes, a person has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. This right is explicitly stated in Article 22(1) of the GDPR.

The right to data portability gives the data subject the right to receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format and to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from the original controller, where technically feasible. This right applies when the processing is based on consent or a contract and is carried out by automated means.

A controller should respond to a data subject's access request without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request. This period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests.

Small companies, defined as those employing fewer than 250 persons, are generally exempt from the obligation to keep records of processing activities under Article 30(5) of the GDPR, unless the processing they carry out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.

Data protection by design and by default requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that only necessary personal data are processed by default. These measures should cover the amount of data collected, their processing, storage period, and accessibility. Additionally, providers of AI systems should consider these principles when developing and designing such systems, ensuring that data protection obligations can be met. (Sources: [2], [3])

Pseudonymisation means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person.
Consent to processing can be withdrawn at any time. It should be as easy to withdraw as to give consent (Article 7(3) and Recital 42 of the GDPR).

A contract between a controller and a processor must set out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects. It should also stipulate that the processor processes the personal data only on documented instructions from the controller, ensures that persons authorised to process the personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality, takes all measures required pursuant to Article 32, respects the conditions referred to in paragraphs 2 and 4 for engaging another processor, assists the controller by appropriate technical and organisational measures, and assists the controller in ensuring compliance with the obligations pursuant to Articles 32 to 36. Additionally, at the choice of the controller, the processor should delete or return all the personal data to the controller after the end of the provision of services relating to processing, and delete existing copies unless Union or Member State law requires storage of the personal data.

Yes, personal data can be transferred to a third country that has an adequacy decision. Such transfers do not require any specific authorisation, provided that the Commission has decided that the third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within that third country, or the international organisation in question ensures an adequate level of protection.

The AI Act does not change or override the GDPR. The AI Act is complementary to existing Union law, including the GDPR, and does not affect the obligations of providers and deployers of AI systems in their role as data controllers or processors stemming from Union or national law on the protection of personal data. Data subjects continue to enjoy all the rights and guarantees awarded to them by the GDPR, including the rights related to solely automated individual decision-making, including profiling.

Yes, if any of the obligations laid down in Article 27 of the AI Act are already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the deployer may, when conducting the fundamental rights impact assessment referred to in Article 27(1), include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment or include relevant parts thereof in the fundamental rights impact assessment. However, this does not exempt the deployer from conducting a fundamental rights impact assessment.

Yes, an AI provider may process sensitive personal data such as ethnicity to detect bias in a high-risk AI system, provided that the conditions and safeguards set out in Article 4a(1) and (2) of the AI Act are met. These include ensuring that the processing is strictly necessary, that other data cannot effectively fulfill the purpose, and that appropriate technical and security measures are in place to protect the data.

The AI Act and GDPR both apply to the bank's use of an AI credit scoring system. The AI Act addresses the design, development, and use of AI systems, including the obligations of providers and deployers. The GDPR, particularly Recital 71, covers the right of data subjects not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which have legal effects or significantly affect them. In this case, the bank's AI system producing a decision to reject a loan application could be considered such a decision, and the data subject would have the right not to be subject to this decision without human intervention, unless the decision is expressly authorized by Union or Member State law.

According to the AI Act and the GDPR, biometric data is defined as data allowing for the authentication, identification or categorisation of natural persons and for the recognition of emotions of natural persons. This definition is derived from Article 4, point (14) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 3, point (18) of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Article 3, point (13) of Directive (EU) 2016/680, as referenced in Recital 14 of the AI Act.

From 2 August 2030, providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended to be used by public authorities shall take the necessary steps to comply with the requirements and obligations laid down in this Regulation.

High-risk requirements apply to AI systems that are safety components of products under Annex I of the AI Act when the product undergoes a third-party conformity assessment procedure pursuant to the relevant Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. This is specified in Article 6(1) of the AI Act, which states that such AI systems shall be considered high-risk if they meet the conditions outlined in points (a) and (b) of that article.

The AI literacy obligation requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and others dealing with the operation and use of AI systems. These measures should be tailored to the technical knowledge, experience, education, and training of the individuals involved, as well as the context in which the AI systems are used. The obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy for individuals.
By 2 August 2027, each Member State must ensure that their competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, which shall be operational by that date.

Yes, the AI Act prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts, or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities, without that person’s freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent for that generation or manipulation.

SMEs, including start-ups, may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner, provided that they do not have partner enterprises or linked enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC.

Providers of AI systems, including generative AI systems, that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026.
Fines for SMCs under the AI Act are capped at the lower of the percentages or amounts specified in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 of Article 99(6a).

Yes, a fundamental rights impact assessment can reuse parts of a GDPR data protection impact assessment. According to Article 27(4) of the AI Act, if any of the obligations laid down in this Article is already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of the GDPR, the deployer may, when conducting the fundamental rights impact assessment, include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment or include relevant parts thereof in the fundamental rights impact assessment.

The new prohibitions on AI-generated intimate images and child sexual abuse material, as described in Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb) of the AI Act, are applicable from 2 December 2027 for high-risk AI systems classified as such according to Article 6(2) and Annex III. For other high-risk AI systems classified as such according to Article 6(1) and Annex I, these prohibitions will apply from 2 August 2028.

En personuppgiftsincident ska anmälas till tillsynsmyndigheten inom 72 timmar efter att den personuppgiftsansvarige har fått vetskap om incidenten, om det inte är osannolikt att incidenten inte medför en risk för fysiska personers rättigheter och friheter. Om anmälan inte görs inom 72 timmar, ska den åtföljas av en motivering till förseningen.

Den högsta sanktionsavgiften för förbjudna AI-metoder enligt AI-förordningen är upp till 35 000 000 EUR eller, om överträdelsen begås av ett företag, upp till 7 % av dess totala globala årsomsättning för det föregående räkenskapsåret, beroende på vilket som är högst.
En arbetsgivare får inte använda AI för att avläsa anställdas känslor på arbetsplatsen, eftersom detta utgör ett förbudat AI-användningsområde enligt artikel 5(1)f) i AI-förordningen.

Kraven för AI-system med hög risk enligt bilaga III börjar tillämpas från och med den 2 december 2027 för AI-system som klassificeras som AI-system med hög risk enligt artikel 6.2 och bilaga III, och från och med den 2 augusti 2028 för AI-system som klassificeras som AI-system med hög risk enligt artikel 6.1 och bilaga I.

Vid erbjudande av informationssamhällets tjänster direkt till ett barn, ska vid tillämpningen av artikel 6.1 a behandling av personuppgifter som rör ett barn vara tillåten om barnet är minst 16 år. Om barnet är under 16 år ska sådan behandling vara tillåten endast om och i den mån samtycke ges eller godkänns av den person som har föräldraansvar för barnet.

En leverantör enligt AI-förordningen är en fysisk eller juridisk person, en offentlig myndighet, en byrå eller ett annat organ som utvecklar ett AI-system eller en AI-modell för allmänna ändamål eller som låter utveckla ett AI-system eller en AI-modell för allmänna ändamål och släpper ut det eller den på marknaden eller tar AI-systemet i bruk i eget namn eller under eget varumärke, antingen mot betalning eller kostnadsfritt.

En chattbot som interagerar direkt med fysiska personer måste informeras om att den interagerar med ett AI-system, om det inte är uppenbart för en fysisk person som är normalt informerad och skäligen uppmärksam och medveten. Denna skyldighet är inte tillämplig på AI-system som upptäcker, förebyggar, förhindrar, utredar eller lagför brott enligt lag.

En AI-modell för allmänna ändamål ska förutsättas ha kapacitet med hög påverkansgrad enligt punkt 1 a om den sammanlagda beräkningsmängd som används för dess träning mätt i flyttalsberäkningar är större än 10^25.

En registrerad har rätt att få sina personuppgifter raderade om de inte längre behövs med tanke på de ändamål för vilka de samlats in eller på annat sätt behandlats, om den registrerade återkallar sitt samtycke, om den invänder mot behandlingen, om behandlingen av personuppgifterna på annat sätt inte överensstämmer med denna förordning, eller om personuppgifterna måste raderas för att uppfylla en rättslig förpliktelse. Ytterligare skäl för radering inkluderar att personuppgifterna har behandlats på olagligt sätt, eller att personuppgifterna har samlats in i samband med erbjudande av informationssamhällets tjänster.

En konsekvensbedömning avseende dataskydd ska särskilt krävas i följande fall: a) En systematisk och omfattande bedömning av fysiska personers personliga aspekter som grundar sig på automatisk behandling, inbegripet profilering, och på vilken beslut grundar sig som har rättsliga följder för fysiska personer eller på liknande sätt i betydande grad påverkar fysiska personer. b) Behandling i stor omfattning av särskilda kategorier av uppgifter, som avses i artikel 9.1, eller av personuppgifter som rör fällande domar i brottmål och lagöverträdelser som innefattar brott, som avses i artikel 10. c) Systematisk övervakning av en allmän plats i stor omfattning. (Sources: [2], [3], [4])

En myndighet måste utse ett dataskyddsombud om den genomför behandlingar som uppfyller vissa kriterier, t.ex. om den behandlar personuppgifter som rör fällande domar i brottmål och lagöverträdelser som innefattar brott, eller om den är en del av domstolarnas dömande verksamhet. I andra fall än de som avses i artikel 37(1) punkt a) och b), kan en enda dataskyddsombud utnämnas för flera myndigheter eller organ, med hänsyn till deras organisationsstruktur och storlek, enligt artikel 37(3).

Ja, en AI-system som används för att sortera jobbansökningar kan klassificeras som ett AI-system med hög risk eftersom det påverkar framtida karriärutsikter och arbetstagares rättigheter. Denna klassificering baseras på AI Act Recital 57.

Tillhandahållare av AI-system med hög risk ska spara de loggar som genereras automatiskt av det AI-systemet med hög risk, i den mån sådana loggar står under deras kontroll, under en period som är lämplig för det avsedda ändamålet med AI-systemet med hög risk, dock i minst sex månader, om inte annat föreskrivs i tillämplig unionsrätt eller nationell rätt, i synnerhet unionsrätten om skydd av personuppgifter.

Leverantörer och tillhandahållare av AI-system ska vidta åtgärder för att främja utvecklingen av AI-kunnighet hos sin personal och andra personer som för deras räkning arbetar med drift och användning av AI-system. Denna skyldighet kräver inte att leverantörer eller tillhandahållare garanterar någon viss nivå av AI-kunnighet hos enskilda personer.
Insufficient

The Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) requires providers of very large online platforms or very large online search engines to identify and mitigate systemic risks that may arise from the dissemination of content that has been artificially generated or manipulated, particularly regarding the risk of negative effects on democratic processes, civic discourse, and electoral processes, including through disinformation. However, the AI Act and GDPR texts provided do not directly answer the specific requirements of the Digital Services Act regarding illegal content.

The fees for testing and assessment activities shall be levied on the provider of a high-risk AI system who has applied for a third-party conformity assessment to the Commission. The provider shall pay the costs related to the services entrusted by the Commission to the notified bodies in accordance with this Article directly to the notified body.
Insufficient
Insufficient

The maximum fine under the UK GDPR after Brexit is up to 10,000,000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is based on Article 83(4) of the GDPR, which applies to infringements of certain provisions related to the obligations of controllers and processors.
Insufficient

The AI Act does not specify that CEN-CENELEC is the sole or primary entity for publishing harmonised standards. The publication of harmonised standards is mentioned in the context of the Official Journal of the European Union, but it does not detail the specific bodies responsible for such publications.
Insufficient

Varje medlemsstat utseende en anmälande myndighet och en marknadskontrollmyndighet för att utöva tillsyn avseende tillämpningen och genomförandet av AI-förordningen. I Sverige skulle denna tillsyn generellt utövas av nationella behöriga myndigheter, vilka kan vara valfri typ av offentlig enhet enligt specifika nationella organisatoriska särdrag och behov.
Insufficient

The training-compute threshold above which an AI system becomes high-risk under the AI Act is not explicitly stated in the provided sources. The sources mention that a general-purpose AI model that meets the applicable threshold for high-impact capabilities should be presumed to be a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk, but the specific threshold is not defined.
The GDPR does not specifically require a fundamental rights impact assessment for AI systems. The AI Act (Article 27) mandates this assessment, not the GDPR.

No, shops cannot use facial recognition for security purposes as it falls under the prohibition of creating or expanding facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage, which is explicitly prohibited under Recital 43 of the AI Act.

qwen2.5_7b__rag__graph.answer: An AI system is defined as a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment. It infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments, for explicit or implicit objectives.

A 'deployer' under the AI Act is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity.

A 'provider' in the AI Act means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge.

Social scoring of people by AI systems is not allowed under the AI Act. Such systems may lead to discriminatory outcomes and the exclusion of certain groups, violating the right to dignity and non-discrimination. They are therefore prohibited.

No, the use of AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the areas of workplace and education institutions is prohibited, except where the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons.

The use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage is prohibited according to Recital 43 and Article 5(1)(e) of the AI Act.

Police may use real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for the following purposes: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings, or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons; (iii) the genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty for offences referred to in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or a detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.

An AI system that is a safety component of a product is considered high-risk if both conditions are fulfilled: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or the AI system is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) the product whose safety component is the AI system, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment, with a view to the placing on the market or the putting into service of that product pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I.

An AI system listed in Annex III is not considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety, or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making. This can occur if the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task, improve the result of a previously completed human activity, detect decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing human assessment, or perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the use cases listed in Annex III. However, the AI system shall always be considered high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons.

An AI tool that screens and filters job applications is considered a high-risk AI system under the AI Act, as it is intended to be used for recruitment or selection of natural persons, which is one of the categories listed in Annex III, point 4(a).

A risk management system for a high-risk AI system must include the identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, the estimation and evaluation of risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, the evaluation of other risks based on data from post-market monitoring, and the adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures. These measures should aim to eliminate or reduce risks as far as technically feasible, and provide information and, where appropriate, training to deployers.

Training, validation, and testing data sets for high-risk AI systems must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They should have the appropriate statistical properties, including as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. These characteristics can be met at the level of individual data sets or at the level of a combination thereof.
Yes, high-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.

The purpose of human oversight for high-risk AI systems is to prevent or minimise the risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may emerge when such systems are used, particularly when risks persist despite the application of other requirements. This includes enabling the deployer to properly understand the system's capacities and limitations, monitor its operation, detect and address anomalies, and intervene as necessary.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data. For financial institutions subject to Union financial services law, the logs must be maintained as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant financial service law.

Deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III are required to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment.

Yes, a chatbot must inform users that they are interacting with an AI system, unless it is obvious from the context that the interaction is with an AI. This obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards.

Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. However, this obligation does not apply where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, and the transparency obligations are limited to disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work.
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 10^25.

Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation, which shall contain, at a minimum, the information set out in Annex XI. This documentation should be made available, upon request, to the AI Office and national competent authorities. Additionally, providers must draw up, keep up-to-date, and make available information and documentation to providers of AI systems who intend to integrate the general-purpose AI model into their AI systems. This information should enable providers of AI systems to have a good understanding of the capabilities and limitations of the general-purpose AI model and to comply with their obligations pursuant to this Regulation. The information and documentation should contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex XII. Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must also comply with the additional obligations listed in Articles 55 and 54, including the performance of model evaluation and the assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks.

The maximum fine for using a prohibited AI practice is up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher.

A fine of up to EUR 7 500 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 1 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, applies for giving misleading information to a notified body under the AI Act.

The Commission may impose on providers of general-purpose AI models fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher.

The provider must report a serious incident caused by a high-risk AI system immediately after establishing a causal relationship, but not later than 10 days after becoming aware of the incident. However, in the event of a widespread infringement or a serious incident, the report must be provided immediately, and not later than two days after becoming aware of it.

Yes, the AI Act applies to AI systems used exclusively for military purposes if they are used for other purposes temporarily or permanently. According to Recital 24, if an AI system developed, placed on the market, put into service, or used for military, defence, or national security purposes is used outside those temporarily or permanently for other purposes, such as civilian or humanitarian purposes, law enforcement, or public security purposes, it falls within the scope of this Regulation.
An AI model developed only for scientific research and development is excluded from the scope of the AI Act according to Article 2(6) and Recital 25 of the AI Act.

Yes, a person affected by a decision based on a high-risk AI system has the right to an explanation. This right is provided under Article 86(1) of the AI Act, which states that any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of systems listed under point 2 thereof, and which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights, shall have the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken.

The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system must contain, at a minimum, the elements set out in Annex IV. These elements include general characteristics, capabilities, and limitations of the system, algorithms, data, training, testing, and validation processes used, as well as documentation on the relevant risk-management system. It should be clear and comprehensive and kept up to date throughout the lifetime of the AI system.

For a high-risk biometric AI system, where the provider has applied harmonised standards, the provider shall opt for the assessment of the quality management system and the assessment of the technical documentation, with the involvement of a notified body, referred to in Annex VII. This is because high-risk AI systems intended to be used for biometrics are an exception to the general rule and should be carried out as a general rule by the provider under its own responsibility, with the only exception of AI systems intended to be used for biometrics, which require the involvement of a notified body.

A provider of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III, has to register themselves and their system in the EU database. Additionally, if the provider concludes that the AI system is not high-risk according to Article 6(3), they also need to register themselves and the system in the EU database.

The post-market monitoring system of a high-risk AI system must actively and systematically collect, document, and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or collected through other sources on the performance of the AI system throughout its lifetime. This data should allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of the AI system with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. Additionally, where relevant, the system should include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems.

Providers of high-risk AI systems are required to ensure compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2, indicate their contact information, have a quality management system in place, keep relevant documentation and logs, undergo conformity assessment, affix the CE marking, comply with registration obligations, take corrective actions, demonstrate conformity upon request, and ensure accessibility. These obligations are detailed in Articles 16, 17, 20, and 21 of the AI Act.
The controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority.

Data subjects must be told about a personal data breach without undue delay when the breach is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms (Article 34(1)). However, if appropriate technical and organizational measures are in place, such as encryption, or if subsequent measures have been taken to mitigate the risk, or if notifying the data subject would involve disproportionate effort, then the data subject does not need to be notified immediately (Article 34(3)).

The maximum GDPR fine for violating the basic principles of processing, such as lawfulness, fairness, and transparency (Article 5(1)(a)), is up to 20,000,000 EUR, or 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 83(5)).

Administrative fines for controllers who breach their obligations on data protection by design or on records of processing, as outlined in Articles 25 and 30 of the GDPR, can be up to 10,000,000 EUR or 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, as per Article 83(4) of the GDPR.

A data subject can ask for their personal data to be erased based on the following grounds: the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed; the data subject withdraws consent; the data subject objects to the processing; the personal data have been unlawfully processed; the personal data have to be erased for compliance with a legal obligation; or the personal data have been collected in relation to the offer of information society services. (Sources: [1], [2], [5])

It is mandatory to designate a data protection officer in cases where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity; the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10.

A data protection impact assessment is required when a type of processing, particularly using new technologies, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Additionally, it is mandatory for systematic and extensive evaluations of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, and decisions based on such evaluations; processing on a large scale of special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences; and systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas on a large scale. These requirements are outlined in Articles 35(1), 35(3), and 35(10) of the GDPR.

From the age of 16, a child can consent on their own to the processing of their data by an online service. For children below 16, consent must be given or authorised by the holder of parental responsibility over the child.

The lawful bases for processing personal data include: (a) consent of the data subject; (b) necessity for performance of a contract or steps prior to contract formation; (c) compliance with a legal obligation; (d) protection of vital interests of the data subject or another natural person; (e) performance of a task in the public interest or exercise of official authority; and (f) pursuit of legitimate interests of the controller or third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights of the data subject. These bases are outlined in Article 6(1) of the GDPR.

Special categories of personal data include health data, genetic data, biometric data, and data concerning sex life or sexual orientation. These categories are subject to higher protection and specific conditions for processing under both the GDPR and the AI Act.

Yes, a person has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning him or her or similarly significantly affects him or her. This right is explicitly stated in Article 22(1) of the GDPR.

The right to data portability gives the data subject the ability to receive their personal data in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format and to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from the original controller, where technically feasible (Article 20(2)). This right applies when the processing is based on consent or a contract (Article 20(1)).

The controller should respond to a data subject's access request without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request. This period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests.

Small companies, employing fewer than 250 persons, are generally exempt from maintaining records of processing activities under Article 30 of the GDPR, unless the processing they carry out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences.

Data protection by design and by default requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that only necessary personal data are processed by default. These measures should cover the amount of data collected, the extent of their processing, storage periods, and accessibility. Additionally, controllers must integrate data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, into their processing activities. (Sources: [2], [3])

Pseudonymisation means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person. (Source: [2])

Yes, consent to processing can be withdrawn at any time. The withdrawal of consent shall not affect the lawfulness of processing based on consent before its withdrawal. Prior to giving consent, the data subject shall be informed thereof. It shall be as easy to withdraw as to give consent.

A contract between a controller and a processor must contain, at a minimum, the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects. The processor must also ensure that persons authorised to process the personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality, and take all measures required pursuant to Article 32. The processor must assist the controller in ensuring compliance with the obligations pursuant to Articles 32 to 36, taking into account the nature of processing and the information available to the processor. Additionally, the processor must assist the controller by appropriate technical and organisational measures, insofar as this is possible, for the fulfilment of the controller's obligation to respond to requests for exercising the data subject's rights laid down in Chapter III. The contract may also be based on standard contractual clauses referred to in paragraphs 7 and 8 of Article 28, and must be in writing, including in electronic form.

Yes, personal data can be transferred to a third country that has an adequacy decision. Such transfers do not require any specific authorisation, provided that the Commission has decided that the third country, a territory or one or more specified sectors within that third country, or the international organisation in question ensures an adequate level of protection.

The AI Act does not change or override the GDPR. According to Article 2(7) of the AI Act, Union law on the protection of personal data, privacy and the confidentiality of communications applies to personal data processed in connection with the rights and obligations laid down in this Regulation. This means that the AI Act does not affect the application of the GDPR or other relevant Union laws governing the processing of personal data.

Yes, if the obligations laid down in Article 27 of the AI Act are already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the deployer may, when conducting the fundamental rights impact assessment referred to in Article 27(1), include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment or include relevant parts thereof in the fundamental rights impact assessment. However, the fundamental rights impact assessment is still required.

Yes, an AI provider may process sensitive personal data such as ethnicity to detect bias in a high-risk AI system, provided that the conditions and safeguards set out in Article 4a(1) and (2) of the AI Act are met. These conditions include ensuring that the processing is strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, and that appropriate technical and organisational measures are in place to protect the data.

The AI credit scoring system used by the bank falls under the scope of the AI Act, as it is a high-risk AI system intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity (credit assessment). The bank must comply with the transparency obligations under Article 50(3) of the AI Act, informing the natural persons (loan applicants) of the operation of the system and processing their personal data in accordance with the GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725).

The AI Act and the GDPR define 'biometric data' in a similar manner. According to the AI Act (Article 3(34)) and the GDPR (Article 4(14)), biometric data means personal data resulting from specific technical processing relating to the physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a natural person, such as facial images or dactyloscopic data.

The obligations for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III apply from 2 December 2027 for systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, and from 2 August 2028 for systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I.

High-risk requirements apply to AI systems that are safety components of products under Annex I of the AI Act when the product undergoes a third-party conformity assessment procedure pursuant to the relevant Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I. This is specified in Article 6(1) of the AI Act, which states that such AI systems shall be considered high-risk if they meet the conditions outlined in points (a) and (b) of that article.

Providers and deployers of AI systems are required to take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. These measures should consider the technical knowledge, experience, education, and training of the individuals, as well as the context in which the AI systems are to be used. However, this obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy for any individual.
By 2 August 2027, each Member State must ensure that their competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, which shall be operational by that date.

Yes, the AI Act prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts, or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities, without that person’s freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent for that generation or manipulation; (Article 5(1)(ba), Source [1]).

SMEs, including start-ups, may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner, provided that they do not have partner enterprises or linked enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC.

Providers of AI systems, including generative AI systems, that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026.
Fines for SMCs under the AI Act are capped at the lower of the percentages or amounts specified in paragraphs 3, 4, and 5 of Article 99(6a).

Yes, a fundamental rights impact assessment can reuse parts of a GDPR data protection impact assessment. According to Article 27(4) of the AI Act, if any of the obligations laid down in this Article is already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of the GDPR, the deployer may, when conducting the fundamental rights impact assessment, include cross-references to the relevant sections of that data protection impact assessment or include relevant parts thereof in the fundamental rights impact assessment.

The new prohibitions on AI-generated intimate images and child sexual abuse material, as described in Article 5(1)(ba) of the AI Act, are applicable from 2 August 2025. This is based on the fact that the general provisions of the AI Act, including Article 5, are set to apply from 2 August 2025, as stated in Article 113(b) of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) [2].

The AI Act does not specify a training-compute threshold above which an AI system becomes high-risk. Instead, it focuses on the high-impact capabilities and systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models. Recital 112 mentions that a general-purpose AI model that meets the applicable threshold for high-impact capabilities should be presumed to be a high-risk AI system, but it does not provide a specific numerical threshold.
The GDPR does not specifically require a fundamental rights impact assessment for AI systems. The AI Act (Article 27) mandates this assessment, not the GDPR.

The AI Act does not ban all biometric identification. Article 5(1)(h) of the AI Act allows the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for specific law enforcement purposes, such as the targeted search for specific victims or the prevention of imminent threats. However, this use is subject to strict conditions, including the necessity for one of the specified objectives. Shops using facial recognition for security purposes would need to ensure their use falls under one of these exceptions.
